newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal moves to speed Nazi gold probe.
newsitem.headline: Portugal moves to speed Nazi gold probe.

text.p: Stung by suggestions of foot-dragging, Portugal's central bank is setting up a special commission to speed a probe into Nazi gold the country acquired during World War Two.

Bank of Portugal governor Antonio de Sousa said the commission would include members of Portugal's Jewish community and that it would assist an economic historian already at work investigating gold purchases by Portugal during and shortly before the 1939-45 war.
"Nobody is more interested than we are that the information is available as soon as possible," de Sousa told journalists on Thursday night.

While international attention has focused on the role of Switzerland as a haven and channel for Nazi funds, Portugal has also come under the spotlight after documents released recently in the United States showed it received significant quantities of gold.
The suspicion is that the gold came from the looted reserves of the Belgian and Dutch central banks after their countries were overrun by Nazi forces at the start of the war.
There is also the highly sensitive question of what happened to gold stolen from concentration camp victims and melted down by the Nazi regime.

The normally reserved central bank responded by announcing last December that it had asked economic historian Joaquim Costa Leite to draw up a report on the bank's dealings during the war years. But it set no deadline for the study and said it would have to stick rigidly to Portugal's tight bank secrecy laws.
The move was criticised as being too little and too slow, particularly by the Nazi-hunting Simon Wiesenthal Centre which pressed the bank to throw open its archives to more investigators.

De Sousa said that the special commission, probably made up of around five people, would have the role of receiving and probing specific questions so that they could be answered quickly rather than wait for the full Leite report which should be ready in October.
"The idea is to accelerate the process," De Sousa said.

The governor said the Bank would in any case be in a position within the next one to two months to release some general information about flows of gold during the period, including who were the buyers and sellers.

He said that investigations so far refuted one charge raised by the Simon Wiesenthal Centre -- that Portugal had been a principal channel for gold, presumably Nazi gold, shipped to Argentina during the latter years of the war.
Although officially neutral, Portugal was under right-wing dictatorship during the war years and its government did little to hide its sympathies for Germany and its allies.

The Centre's European director Shimon Samuels told journalists after a visit to Lisbon last week that Portugal had shipped some 3.5 tonnes of gold, worth some $38 million at today's prices, in just 12 months between 1942 and 1943.
"There were no shipments of gold to Argentina," said De Sousa. In fact, Portugal bought gold from Argentina during the period and the amounts fitted perfectly with those detailed by Samuels.
Bank officials said that Samuels, who made his charge following a visit to Argentina, must have misinterpreted the central bank records in Buenos Aires.

De Sousa also rejected suggestions that Portugal's gold reserves had risen in an unusual fashion during the war years. He said that Portugal bought some 300 tonnes in the decade to 1945, little different from the 320 bought in the following 10 years or the 290 tonnes acquired between 1955 and 1965.
"Portugal had a policy of acquiring gold but the rhythm of purchases was very steady over the three decades," he said.
